questions.problem: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=x-1,$ then ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159116/assets/24683f81da1c7e90ccbd51748f5f46407137be4a40ef5f0678292b70f0781eff.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2} & =x-1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x+2)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159116/assets/e955ad94bca70a8e6f996d81814ffa8fcc7a322d5979db7b0726d39558b6aa86.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{e}^{y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}-{e}^{0})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x(x-1)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx & ={[{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(64-24)-(1-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =40+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}8x{y}^{3}\,dA,\,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and below the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $y\le 0,$ we obtain

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\,⟹\,y=-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}.
$$

Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159116/assets/9c6b1dd7d81d124888ddd588027eed908a0eaecb2c42ebc79f3253c4123dbe86.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the circle with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$-1\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159116/assets/bd584d7481549b792e786a7186ba7ee87cd536258c5a0135f36ee17d96c4880d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\le y\le 0\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}8x{y}^{3}\,dA={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x[{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}4{y}^{3}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x{[{y}^{4}]}_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x(0-{(-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx & ={[\frac{(1-{x}^{2})^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{(1-{1}^{2})^{3}}{3}-\frac{(1-(-1)^{2})^{3}}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{ }x(y-1)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\text{ }(y-1)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y]}_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(\frac{1}{2}(1-{x}^{2})-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}(1-{x}^{2})-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(-2\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}-2x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\,dx & ={[\frac{2(1-{x}^{2})^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =0-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$

$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4x\,dx & ={[2{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2{(\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$
